newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary ministry sees widening trade gap in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Hungary ministry sees widening trade gap in 1997.

text.p: Improving performance in Hungary's industrial output and investments this year is likely to widen the trade gap compared with 1996, the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Tourism (IKIM) said on Wednesday.
But a larger gap is not seen boosting the current account deficit and the country's indebtedness, the ministry added.
"Higher production and investments is to come along with larger demand for imports," IKIM Deputy Secretary of State Lajos Berenyi told a news conference.

"We forecast exports to increase by 10 percent and imports by 11 to 12 percent this year," he said. "Due to the larger growth in imports, the trade gap will be between $3 and $3.5 billion this year, which is up from $2.7 billion last year."
Hungary's exports rose by 13 percent in 1996, while imports increased by 12 percent.
Berenyi added that the ministry expected industrial output to rise by four to five percent percent in 1998, while investments in industrial production should grow at an even higher rate.
According to Central Statistical Office (KSH) figures, industrial output rose by 2.3 percent in 1996 compared with 1995, while investments fell three percent.
The main factor encouraging industrial production growth this year will be the expansion of exports, while increasing imports should support investments and not household consumption, Berenyi said.

He added that the widening trade gap was not likely to affect the current account as tourism would probably produce the same surplus, $1.3 billion, this year as in 1996 and the inflow of foreign capital was not seen slowing.

He said a larger than expected growth in household consumption could threaten the current account balance only if the government would soften its economic policies steering between encouraging growth and preserving stability.
"Higher industrial production also comes along with higher exports," he added. "If the economic policy insists on growth and stability together, exports must grow quicker than now."

Real wages are expected to stagnate or rise slightly this year after a slump of five percent in 1996, while the government targets gross domestic product (GDP) growth of two to three percent in 1997, up from some one percent in 1996.
Average net monthly wage in the business sector rose by 5.9 percent in the January-February period year on year in real terms, the KSH said on Tuesday.
Berenyi said that household consumption did not boost imports in the first two months of the year.
"In the goods groups suitable for household consumtion I did not find the trace of imports growth." -- Budapest newsroom (36 1) 327 4040
